claims.arxiv2606_28153: In two aligned chat models, a jailbreak that succeeds does not wipe out the model's internal representation of harm; it routes around it. Components that carry the refusal decision are knocked down, while other safety-relevant attention heads stay active even on the attacks that work. A safety-relevant head counts as attack-resistant if its activation distributions for refused harmful requests and for successful attacks overlap by at least 0.5, and as compromised if that overlap is below 0.5 and its standardised activation falls under attack. Knocking down a small set of heads counts as a sufficient local route to bypassing refusal if suppressing at most eight of them lifts attack success from roughly 0% to at least 80%, with non-overlapping 95% intervals against suppressing the same number of heads chosen at random. The surviving representation has practical value if, with no extra training, reading it classifies harmful inputs better than the model's own refusal behaviour and matches or beats the strongest purpose-built safety classifier on aggregate Macro-F1.
claims.arxiv2606_28153_c1: The safety signal that survives a successful jailbreak in these models is held up in part by a distinct population of middle-layer attention heads, and the heads that get knocked down are knocked down by the tokens of the jailbreak wrapper rather than by the harmful request inside it. Supported only if suppressing the surviving heads during successful attacks cuts mean absolute middle-layer safety activation by at least 10% against leaving them alone, and if, when each head's activation is attributed back to input tokens, the tokens of the harmful request push both populations the same way while the wrapper tokens push them in opposite directions.

0.text: Build matched pairs of refused requests and successful attacks. Setup: benign instructions from a standard instruction set, harmful instructions from several published harmful-behaviour sets, and attack variants generated by four different jailbreak methods, for two aligned 7-8B chat models. Keep only one-to-one pairs where the plain harmful request is refused and its attacked version succeeds, so every comparison holds the underlying request fixed. Result: from roughly 10,000 attack samples, 378 pairs survive for one model and 176 for the other, a yield of about 2-3%.

1.text: Extract the refusal direction and fix the rule for sorting heads. Setup: take a difference-in-means direction between harmful and benign instructions, pick the layer on a validation set (layer 12 for one model, 14 for the other) and normalise it. Project it back through each attention head's output circuit, read each head's activation at the end-of-instruction position on benign, refused-harmful and successful-attack inputs, estimate the distributions by kernel density, and set both overlap thresholds to 0.5. Standardise each head against its benign mean and spread; among heads that separate harmful from benign, call a low-overlap head compromised if its activation falls under attack and surviving if it rises.

2.text: Does a successful attack flatten the refusal feature across the model? Setup: measure activation of the chosen direction at the end-of-instruction token across attention heads and MLP blocks, for refused harmful inputs and their successful attack variants, in both models. Result: attacks reduce some components but leave substantial activation in the middle layers, including layers earlier work identified as safety-relevant, rather than removing the feature model-wide.

3.text: Identify the two head populations. Setup: apply the two-stage overlap rule at thresholds of 0.5 to 416 heads in the first 13 layers of one model and 480 heads in the first 15 of the other. Result: 80 harm-salient heads for one model, of which 21 compromised and 17 surviving; 43, 20 and 19 for the other. More than 60% of the compromised heads sit in layers 0-3, while the surviving ones spread through layers 5-12. Attacks produce both strong decreases early and strong increases in the middle, not a uniform reduction.

4.text: Does the split depend on where the overlap threshold is drawn? Setup: set both stages to the same threshold and sweep it from 0.1 to 0.9. Result: counts move smoothly and the qualitative split holds between 0.4 and 0.6; at 0.5 one model gives 80 harm-salient, 17 surviving, 21 compromised and the other 43, 19, 20. At the extremes the rule degenerates, giving no heads of either kind at 0.1 and equal numbers of both at 0.9.

5.text: Does the density-estimation setting determine the assignment? Setup: scale the kernel bandwidth by factors from 0.2 to 2.0, recompute every overlap, rerun the filter at fixed 0.5 thresholds, and compare the resulting head sets with the default by Jaccard overlap and rank correlation. Result: rank correlation stays at or above 0.93 across the whole sweep and above 0.99 for factors between 0.8 and 1.4; Jaccard overlap is 0.81 to 1.00 in that middle band but falls to 0.43-0.68 at the extreme setting of 2.0.

6.text: Is knocking down the compromised heads enough to bypass refusal? Setup: on harmful inputs the model normally refuses, where baseline attack success is about 0%, subtract a fixed multiple of the refusal direction from each selected head's output at the end-of-instruction position, increasing the number of heads treated. The multiplier was chosen because smaller values did little and larger ones destabilised generation. Result: at eight heads, attack success reaches 95.0% and 81.6% for the two models; at the full intervention size, 99.5 +- 0.3% and 83.7 +- 1.1% over 10 runs.

7.text: Would knocking down any heads do the same? Setup: apply the identical intervention to randomly chosen heads, matched in number to the identified compromised set, over 10 seeds with 95% intervals. Result: 4.0 +- 3.7% and 10.2 +- 11.6% attack success, against 99.5 +- 0.3% and 83.7 +- 1.1% for the identified heads, so the intervals do not overlap.

8.text: Does the intervention simply break generation? Setup: inspect generations after intervening on 8 to 21 heads. Result: the text stays coherent and on topic. Caveat: no standard capability benchmark is run on the intervened models, so this rests on inspection rather than measurement.

9.text: Do the surviving heads supply part of the signal that remains after a successful attack? Setup: apply the same suppression to the surviving heads on successful attack inputs and measure mean absolute activation across middle-layer heads. Result: activation falls from 0.0062 to 0.0053 in one model, a 14% drop, against 0.0086 on plain harmful inputs; and from 0.222 to 0.181 in the other, an 18% drop, against 0.397. Both clear the 10% bar.

10.text: Which tokens produce the two populations' opposite responses? Setup: decompose each head's end-of-instruction activation into additive standardised per-token contributions using its attention weights and value projection, then sum separately over the tokens of the original harmful request and over the tokens of the jailbreak wrapper. Result: on the harmful-request tokens the two populations' median contributions sit within 0.15 of each other in both models. On the wrapper tokens they separate, with medians near -1.5 for the compromised heads and +1.5 for the surviving ones, a gap of more than three standard deviations.

11.text: Can the surviving activations classify harmful inputs with no training? Setup: pick observation positions whose benign-versus-harmful overlap is below a threshold, aggregate their standardised activations into a top-m score, and threshold it. One forward pass, no gradients, no intervention, no detector training. Evaluate on ten balanced harmful-versus-benign datasets and report per-dataset and sample-weighted Macro-F1. Result: against each model's own refusal behaviour, weighted Macro-F1 rises from 0.470 to 0.853, 0.514 to 0.816, 0.519 to 0.798, 0.664 to 0.752, 0.797 to 0.888, 0.506 to 0.860 and 0.470 to 0.847 across seven models. Purpose-built classifiers score 0.599, 0.666, 0.877 and 0.880; the best activation reader reaches 0.888, so it edges the strongest of them. On adversarial datasets the gap is largest, with scores of 0.85-0.98 where refusal-based scoring is below 0.5.

13.text: Does the detector earn its score by flagging everything? Setup: evaluate on a benchmark of hard benign prompts that safety systems tend to over-refuse, reporting F1 and specificity on those hard benign cases, against a plain baseline and two other training-free detectors. Result: F1 0.606 and hard specificity 0.418, against 0.571/0.329 for the plain baseline, 0.510/0.053 and 0.453/0.290 for the other two, so it is the best of the training-free group on both. Separately, against those same two training-free detectors on the harmful-detection benchmarks, it reaches 0.856 weighted Macro-F1 against 0.741 and 0.611.

split_changes.13: ADDED to C0 as a control. The paper's appendix D.5 reports an over-refusal evaluation and a training-free baseline comparison that the 18-page cutoff hid from v3. It is a genuine control on the claim's detection bar, since a detector that flagged every hard benign prompt could otherwise score well.
